title: Esther 1:1–9
context: The book opens in the days of Ahasuerus, who reigns from India to Ethiopia over one hundred twenty-seven provinces, and sits at Susa the palace. In the third year he holds a long display of royal wealth, then a seven-day feast for all present in Susa, great and small, while Vashti the queen makes a feast for the women in the royal house. The scene is one of abundance, law, and court custom, not a coded lesson in the hangings and the gold. This book never names God. That silence should be noted at the outset, especially because later readers often infer hidden providence in the turns of the story, but it is not proof that God is absent, and the court description is not a cipher that must be decoded verse by verse. Hidden-providence readings of even this opening, as the setting in which a later deliverance will be prepared, are common in both traditions and remain shared ground, held with a light hand. Ahasuerus is commonly identified with Xerxes I of Persia; the identification is widespread and useful, but it is not stated in the text and should be held as a common judgment, not as a certainty. Both traditions read the unit as a historical court narrative that will open the way for Vashti’s removal and Esther’s rise, without a party contrast over the king’s name or over the book’s silence about God.

verses.text: Now in the days of Ahasuerus (this is Ahasuerus who reigned from India even to Ethiopia, over one hundred twenty-seven provinces),
verses.arminianNotes:
The story is set “in the days of Ahasuerus”, who reigned “from India even to Ethiopia, over one hundred twenty-seven provinces”. The book never names God, already in this first line; the setting is a Persian court, given in royal terms. Ahasuerus is commonly identified with Xerxes I, a judgment held by many readers and consistent with a king who rules a vast empire from Susa, but the text itself gives the Hebrew name and the span of the realm, not the Greek one. Other identifications have been offered. The point should be named and hedged.

Arminian readers take the heading as a real historical frame, a named king and a named reach of power, without turning the 127 provinces into a symbol.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the court as history. The common Xerxes identification may be used with care, and it should not be treated as if the verse had written that name.

Both traditions note the book’s silence about God from the first verse, without reading that silence as proof of absence, and without a contrast over the king’s identity.

verses.text: in those days, when the King Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Susa the palace,
verses.arminianNotes:
In those days King Ahasuerus “sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Susa the palace”. Susa is the royal center from which the story will move; the palace, or citadel, will be the scene of the feasts and, later, of Mordecai’s watch. The verse places the king in secure state before the display that follows.

Arminian readers take Susa as a real royal seat, the setting of the coming decisions, not as a type of a later city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a historical placement: the throne is at Susa, and the narrative will stay close to that court.

Both traditions keep the verse as scene-setting, and they do not read a hidden divine name out of the palace notice.

verses.text: in the third year of his reign, he made a feast for all his princes and his servants; the army of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces being before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the third year of his reign he makes a feast “for all his princes and his servants”, with the army of Persia and Media and the nobles and princes of the provinces before him. The third year will stand later beside the seventh year of 2:16, a gap that is not filled with a campaign history the verse does not give.

Arminian readers take the feast as a real royal assembly in the third year, princes and army present, not as a parable of pride that needs to be decoded here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the year as the text states it and refuse to invent a political purpose beyond the feast the verse describes.

Both traditions read a public banquet at the height of the court, shared ground as narrative setting, without a contrast over the king’s motives.

verses.text: He displayed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honor of his excellent majesty many days, even one hundred eighty days.
verses.arminianNotes:
He displayed “the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honor of his excellent majesty many days, even one hundred eighty days.” The length and the display are given as facts of the feast. The 180 days are not turned into a symbol, and the display is not explained by a theory of Persian policy the text does not state.

Arminian readers take the long showing of wealth as a historical report of royal magnificence, impressive and excessive as it may be, without a moral sermon forced onto the number.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the verse in the register of court narrative. The honor and the many days set the scale of this kingdom, the backdrop against which later weakness and later courage will be seen.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the 180 days or to invent a keyContrast over royal pride.

verses.text: When these days were fulfilled, the king made a seven day feast for all the people who were present in Susa the palace, both great and small, in the court of the garden of the king’s palace.
verses.arminianNotes:
When those days are fulfilled, the king makes “a seven day feast for all the people who were present in Susa the palace, both great and small, in the court of the garden of the king’s palace.” The inner feast of princes is followed by a wider banquet in the garden court. Great and small are both included.

Arminian readers hear a real widening of the feast, the people of Susa now present, still a court scene and not a hidden parable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the seven days as the public close of the long display, set in the garden court of the palace.

Both traditions keep the verse as setting, and they do not find a divine name in the garden or the seven days.

verses.text: There were hangings of white and blue material, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and marble pillars. The couches were of gold and silver, on a pavement of red, white, yellow, and black marble.
verses.arminianNotes:
The court is described in hangings of white and blue, cords of fine linen and purple, silver rings, marble pillars, couches of gold and silver, and a pavement of colored marble. The verse is a picture of luxury. It is not a color code, and it is not a place to look for a concealed reference to God.

Arminian readers take the furnishings as a historical description of the garden court, meant to show the scale of the feast.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the hangings, couches, and pavement as they are written, a report of royal splendor, not a symbol system.

Both traditions refuse to decode the materials verse by verse, and they invent no contrast over the description.

verses.text: They gave them drinks in golden vessels of various kinds, including royal wine in abundance, according to the bounty of the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
They gave drinks “in golden vessels of various kinds, including royal wine in abundance, according to the bounty of the king.” The bounty is royal and public. The abundance prepares the next verse’s notice that drinking was not forced, and, in the following unit, the king will be merry with wine.

Arminian readers take the golden vessels and the abundant wine as part of the same historical feast, generosity on the king’s terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear abundance according to the king’s bounty, a court supplying wine in variety and in quantity, without a hidden meaning in the vessels.

Both traditions keep the line as banquet report and do not moralize it into a separate lesson on drink.

verses.text: In accordance with the law, the drinking was not compulsory; for so the king had instructed all the officials of his house, that they should do according to every man’s pleasure.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In accordance with the law, the drinking was not compulsory; for so the king had instructed all the officials of his house, that they should do according to every man’s pleasure.” Even the drinking is placed under a royal instruction: no one is forced, and each may do as he pleases. The notice belongs to the feast’s order, not to a modern argument about liberty.

Arminian readers take the rule as a real court custom in this scene: the law here is the king’s instruction, and pleasure is allowed within it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a commanded freedom at the table, law and pleasure set side by side in the house of the king, still a narrative detail.

Both traditions leave the verse as a report of how the feast was run, without a party contrast over the word law or the word pleasure.

verses.text: Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women in the royal house which belonged to King Ahasuerus.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women in the royal house which belonged to King Ahasuerus.” A separate feast is held for the women, in the royal house, with Vashti as host. The verse states the fact and does not yet explain her later refusal. The two gatherings, the king’s and the queen’s, stand side by side as the setting of the next unit.

Arminian readers take Vashti’s feast as a real royal banquet for the women, reported soberly, without turning her into a lesson or a type at this first mention.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also place Vashti in the royal house as queen and host, a historical figure whose refusal has not yet been told.

Both traditions introduce her without culture-war framing and without reading a hidden providence into the mere fact of a women’s feast.
